themes.name: Why recurrence had to go
themes.summary: Sets up the task the paper cares about — turning one sequence into another — and the models that dominated it. Recurrent models process a sequence one position at a time, which the paper says blocks parallelism within a training example and stretches the path between distant positions. Convolutional models and attention-based memory networks are the prior attempts to get around this. This comes first because everything the paper proposes is a reaction to it.

themes.name: The shape of the model
themes.summary: The outline of the Transformer before any of the math. It keeps the familiar encoder-decoder frame: an encoder turns the input into representations, a decoder emits output tokens one at a time. Both are stacks of six identical layers, and every sub-layer inside a layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization. Read this to have a map before the parts are filled in.

themes.name: How attention is computed
themes.summary: The one operation the model is built from. Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to a weighted sum of the values, with the weights coming from how well the query matches each key. The paper's version scores with a dot product, divides by the square root of the key dimension, and softmaxes; it then runs eight of these in parallel on lower-dimensional projections and concatenates the results. This is the mechanical core, so it comes before the places it gets used.

themes.name: Where attention is used in the model
themes.summary: The same attention function appears in three places. In the encoder, self-attention lets every position look at every other position in the layer below. In the decoder, the same thing runs with a mask so a position can only see itself and earlier positions, which keeps generation auto-regressive. In between, the decoder attends over the encoder's output, with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

themes.name: Position, embeddings, and the feed-forward layer
themes.summary: The parts of a layer that act on each position on its own. Every layer's second sub-layer is a small two-layer network applied identically at every position, and the input and output embedding matrices are shared with the pre-softmax projection. Because there is no recurrence or convolution, nothing so far tells the model what order the tokens are in, so a fixed sinusoidal vector is added to each input embedding. These pieces complete the layer described in the previous themes.

themes.name: Why self-attention, compared to the alternatives
themes.summary: The paper's argument for the swap, made on three criteria: computation per layer, how many operations must run in sequence rather than in parallel, and the longest path a signal travels between two positions. On the third, self-attention connects any two positions in a constant number of steps, which the paper says should make long-range dependencies easier to learn. For very long sequences it sketches a restricted variant where each position attends only to a nearby window. This sits here because it needs both self-attention and the recurrent and convolutional baselines already on the table.

themes.name: Training the thing
themes.summary: Everything needed to reproduce a trained model: the translation datasets, subword vocabularies built with byte-pair encoding or word pieces, batching by sequence length, and eight GPUs on one machine. The learning rate is not fixed — it ramps up linearly for the first 4000 steps and then decays as the inverse square root of the step. Label smoothing, dropout, and averaging the last several checkpoints round out the recipe, and the code was released as tensor2tensor.

themes.name: What the numbers show
themes.summary: How outputs are produced at test time and what they score. Decoding uses beam search with a length penalty; quality is reported as BLEU, with perplexity and an estimated training FLOP count alongside it so quality can be read against cost. The ablations change one design choice at a time to see which parts matter, and a constituency-parsing experiment tests whether the architecture carries to a different task. This comes last because it is the evidence for the claims made earlier.

themes.name: From one dot product to eight heads
themes.summary: These edges build the attention mechanism from the inside out. Equation (1) defines scaled dot-product attention, which is plain dot-product attention plus one divisor, 1/sqrt(d_k); the paper says it picks the dot product over additive attention for speed, and adds the divisor because large d_k pushes the softmax into a flat region. The MultiHead equation then calls Equation (1) h times in parallel, each head working at width d_k = d_v = d_model/h, which is why h = 8 and 64-wide heads go together. The claim for running h heads instead of one is that a single attention output is an average, and averaging blurs what individual subspaces could have kept separate. Figure 2 draws both halves: Equation (1) as a data-flow box on the left, the h parallel heads on the right.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

themes.name: Where attention is wired into the two stacks
themes.summary: The same multi-head block appears in three places: encoder self-attention over the whole input, masked decoder self-attention, and encoder-decoder attention whose keys and values come from the encoder output. The mask is what separates the second use from the first — forbidden positions get minus infinity before the softmax, so they get zero weight, and that is what keeps generation auto-regressive. Around each attention or feed-forward sub-layer sits the same wrapper: a residual connection and layer normalization, which is where the cited layer-norm formula enters and why every sub-layer and embedding is forced to the single width d_model = 512. Equation (2) defines the other sub-layer, the per-position feed-forward network, and N = 6 fixes how many times the pair is stacked. Figure 1 shows the whole arrangement at once.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

themes.name: Putting order back in
themes.summary: Self-attention treats a sequence as a set, so the model has no idea what order its tokens are in. The paper's fix is a positional encoding added to the input embeddings, and the version it uses is the sinusoid bank of Equation (4) — sines and cosines whose wavelengths form a geometric progression. It also tries learned positional embeddings as the alternative. The paper reports nearly identical results for the two and keeps the sinusoids, hedging that they may extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training. This is the one place where the design has to add back something recurrence supplied for free.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

themes.name: The case against recurrence and convolution
themes.summary: Section 4 sets up three criteria — computational complexity per layer, minimum sequential operations, and maximum path length between positions — and Table 1 turns them into numbers for self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers. The argument is that self-attention needs O(1) sequential operations where an RNN needs O(n), and connects any two positions in one step where a convolutional stack needs several layers, ByteNet growing logarithmically with distance and ConvS2S linearly. Short paths are wanted because long-range dependencies are the stated difficulty in sequence transduction, and Figure 3 shows one such dependency drawn out. The criteria do not agree with each other: cheap layers and parallel layers pull apart, and the restricted r-neighborhood variant buys a cheaper layer by lengthening the path. The paper also concedes that separable convolutions can match the layer cost, and that the O(n^2 · d) claim rests on n staying smaller than d, which depends on how the subword vocabulary is set.

sections.title: Applications of Attention in our Model

themes.name: The recipe is mostly borrowed
themes.summary: Much of the training setup is taken from other papers and used at stated settings rather than re-derived. Weight tying comes from the output-embedding work — one matrix in three roles, encoder input, decoder input, and pre-softmax projection — with the sqrt(d_model) multiplier applied on top. Label smoothing is the cited LSR target mixture at eps = 0.1; the subword vocabularies are BPE with its merge loop and joint source-target vocabulary for English-German, and a 32000-token word-piece vocabulary for English-French; the beam-search length penalty is the cited normalizer set to alpha = 0.6. What the paper adds of its own is the schedule: Equation (3) ramps the learning rate linearly for warmup_steps = 4000 and then decays it as the inverse square root, scaled by d_model, which overrides Adam's own step size. The reported training cost is not measured directly but estimated from GPU count, wall-clock time, and an assumed throughput.

themes.name: What the translation numbers show
themes.summary: Table 2 carries the headline result on WMT 2014 English-German and English-French: the big Transformer's BLEU against prior models including ConvS2S and ensembles, plotted against an estimated training cost, so quality and compute are the two axes. Table 3 varies one thing at a time on the base model — head count in rows (A), key size d_k in rows (B), size and dropout in (C) and (D), positional encoding in (E). The paper reads these as: one head is worse than eight but too many heads also drop off, shrinking d_k hurts and may mean the dot product is too simple a compatibility function, removing residual dropout costs quality, and learned positions make no real difference. Label smoothing is the case where the metrics disagree — it makes perplexity worse and BLEU better, and the paper keeps it. Figures 4 and 5 are offered as suggestive, not conclusive: two heads splitting the reference of "its", and two heads in one layer with visibly different patterns.

themes.name: The parsing test
themes.summary: Constituency parsing is the second task, used to check whether the architecture generalizes past translation. It only works as a sequence transduction problem because parse trees are flattened into token sequences by the cited linearization scheme. Table 4 reports WSJ Section 23 F1 in two regimes: trained on the roughly 40K-sentence WSJ treebank alone, and trained semi-supervised on about 17M additional machine-parsed sentences from the cited corpora. The paper reports beating the BerkeleyParser and most prior work with little task-specific tuning, and names RNNG as the one model it does not beat.
